Detention, Retention, and Infiltration

Follow one storm through storage, controlled release, permanent pool, infiltration, evapotranspiration, treatment, and bypass pathways before judging a stormwater practice by its name.

STORMWATER · UNITED STATES FEDERAL FRAME · ILLUSTRATIVE ROUTES · EDUCATIONAL USE
WORKING PREVIEW · PREVIEW 0.1

Follow one storm through temporary storage, permanent pool, soil, underdrain, overflow, and receiving-water routes before deciding what a practice name means.

IN 30 SECONDS

Start with the water, not the label.

  1. Name what enters and where it can wait.
  2. Trace every surface, subsurface, overflow, and bypass exit.
  3. State the intended objective and the evidence needed to show that route still works.

What should I ask before I call this asset detention, retention, or infiltration?
In 30 seconds

What should I ask before I call this asset detention, retention, or infiltration?

In 30 seconds

Start with the water, not the label. Identify what enters, where it can wait, every route it can leave, the objective the asset was built to serve, and the evidence needed to show that route still works.

02
Where can the same stormwater go in each arrangement?
Route the same storm

Where can the same stormwater go in each arrangement?

Route the same storm

The planned tracer uses one illustrative storm and three unlabeled physical arrangements. It reveals temporary storage and controlled release, permanent pool and displacement, infiltration, evapotranspiration, underdrain discharge, overflow, and bypass as separate routes. The values and routes are authored for instruction, not prediction.

Trace one storm through three water rooms

Reveal storage, release, infiltration, evapotranspiration, underdrain, overflow, and bypass as distinct pathways before showing common practice names.

Model boundary: Qualitative authored routes for instruction. No calibrated rainfall, runoff, hydraulic, infiltration, treatment, groundwater, flood, or compliance prediction.

03
Why do detention and retention seem to mean different things in different places?
Names are clues, not proof

Why do detention and retention seem to mean different things in different places?

Names are clues, not proof

EPA sources use detention consistently for temporary storage and later release, but retention is used in more than one way. One source may mean runoff kept from later surface discharge. Another may mean a permanent pool that remains while new runoff displaces water. The brief will state the intended usage and show the physical route every time.

Check the terminology boundary

The learner identifies which conclusion is supported when an asset is called a retention practice but no route, outlet, or objective has been documented.

LEARNING CHECK

An asset is called a retention basin, but you have no drawing, outlet information, or performance objective. What can the name establish by itself?

Recheck which answer preserves uncertainty without discarding the label as a useful clue.

04
What changes when water crosses into soil or groundwater?
Infiltration crosses a boundary

What changes when water crosses into soil or groundwater?

Infiltration crosses a boundary

The planned cutaway separates surface ponding, filter media, native soil, underdrain, seasonal groundwater, and receiving water. It teaches that captured water may infiltrate, filter, drain, overflow, or interact with groundwater depending on site and design. It does not supply a universal separation or infiltration criterion.

05
Which performance measure answers the question I actually care about?
Performance has more than one measure

Which performance measure answers the question I actually care about?

Performance has more than one measure

A worked comparison separates concentration, discharged volume, and total pollutant load. It helps the learner see why a lower concentration, a lower peak, or a dry surface can each answer a different question and cannot stand in for the whole performance story.

06
What observations would show that the intended pathway has changed?
Condition can change the intended route

What observations would show that the intended pathway has changed?

Condition can change the intended route

The planned evidence trace connects sediment, debris, vegetation, inlets, outlets, erosion, underdrains, ponding, and post-storm observations to hypotheses about blocked, shortened, bypassed, or altered pathways. Observations guide the next question. They do not authorize a diagnosis or repair.

07
Can I describe an unfamiliar practice without overclaiming?
Describe the pathway before naming the practice

Can I describe an unfamiliar practice without overclaiming?

Describe the pathway before naming the practice

The learner receives an unfamiliar asset sketch and completes four fields: inflow, storage or treatment, normal exits, and evidence still needed. The task is complete only when every field is filled without claiming a universal name or performance result.

APPLIED WORK PRODUCT

Describe the unfamiliar stormwater asset without assigning a universal name or performance result.

Trace the route again, then separate what the sketch shows from what still requires evidence.

Sources and scope

This working preview uses current United States federal law, federal regulation, and EPA guidance to explain a pathway-first method. EPA materials document that stormwater terminology varies and that performance can involve timing, volume, concentration, total load, groundwater protection, and maintenance.

This brief cannot determine a real asset's design, capacity, drawdown, infiltration rate, treatment performance, groundwater suitability, maintenance action, or compliance. Those decisions require current drawings, site evidence, approved procedures, applicable permits, and qualified judgment.

A USEFUL NEXT STEP

Take the outline. Build the procedure under control.

Copy this outline into the utility's approved workspace only after the actual asset, applicable authority, and responsible reviewers are identified. It is a review structure, not a maintenance or operating procedure.

Stormwater pathway review outline

  1. Asset identity and intended objectiveIdentify the exact asset, approved drawings, owner, design objective, drainage area, and the question this review must answer.
  2. Inflow and storm boundaryState what enters, the time period or storm condition being reviewed, and any upstream bypass or contributing area.
  3. Storage and treatment zonesIdentify each documented surface, media, soil, permanent-pool, and temporary-storage zone.
  4. Every exit routeList controlled outlets, underdrains, infiltration, evapotranspiration, seepage, overflow, bypass, and receiving-water routes.
  5. Site and groundwater evidenceIdentify soil, seasonal groundwater, contamination, pretreatment, well, karst, and nearby-use questions requiring qualified review.
  6. Condition and maintenance evidenceRecord inlet, outlet, sediment, debris, vegetation, erosion, ponding, underdrain, access, and post-storm observations without diagnosing from one observation.
  7. Performance evidenceState which evidence addresses timing, peak, volume, concentration, total load, treatment, and receiving-water response.
  8. Decision authority and follow-upName who reviews, what remains unknown, which approved procedure applies, and what evidence is required before any action.

WHERE THE BRIEF STOPS

A real SOP is a separate product.

A facility-specific SOP needs controlled inputs, applicable authority review, approved chemicals and equipment, named change authority, monitoring, rollback, safety review, version history, and approvals.

If OWOS builds that later, it should be an authenticated agent workflow. The agent would assemble evidence and route review. It would never invent settings or approve its own work.

BEFORE YOU LEAVE

Carry three things forward.

What changed

You replaced a practice label with an explicit water pathway and performance objective.

What to observe

Trace the inlet, storage, outlet, overflow, soil, groundwater boundary, underdrain, sediment, vegetation, and post-storm response.

What not to assume

A name, dry surface, permanent pool, lower concentration, or missing surface water does not prove the complete pathway or performance.
